howDoI.q: How do I show a hit without a flash, with a number that rises?
How do I make a warning light that blinks slowly?
How do I make a light that glows softly instead of blinking?
How do I fade between scenes instead of flashing?
How do I change the sky a little and hold it?
How do I check that my game does not flash too fast?

pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

Flash Safe is a Starter: a small game that shows a few Game-Maker ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. It has three short levels and nothing in it can cost a life.

Play it first. Then open it in Game-Maker (Edit a copy on the home page keeps the original safe) and read the pages below, which say where each thing is made.

The keys

Left and Right walk. Space jumps. F2 shows your lives, hit points and score.

Why this game is here

Some players can get sick from fast flashing, and some people have seizures from flashing light. A game does not need a flash to look exciting, so the simple rules are:

  • No more than 3 flashes in any one second. A flash is a change to light and back.
  • Avoid big flashes of red.
  • Keep anything that flashes small. A lamp is fine. The whole screen is not.
  • Offer other cues. A sound, a shape, a number or a slow fade says the same thing without a flash.

This game never flashes. Its signs show the wrong way as a still picture, never as the real thing.

pages.head: Level 1: Hit Without a Flash
pages.html:
Level 1: Hit Without a Flash

Three brown burrs hang in the air, prickly like a chestnut husk. Walk into the first one and look and listen: you get a beep, Lami makes an ouch face, a gold -5 rises and goes away, and your hit points go down by 5 (press F2 to see them). That is four ways to say “you were hit,” and none of them is a flash.

A still picture beside the last sign shows the wrong way: a whole screen flashing. It is only a picture, in dull colors, with a slash through it. Jump over the other two burrs, take the four coins and go to the door.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 1 is made

  • A burr is a monster. Open fsafe.mon in the monsters editor and pick monster 3, the burr. It has no path, so it hangs there, and its two pictures (burr0 and burr1) turn slowly, 14 ticks each. Its power is 50, under 100, so touching Lami destroys it.
  • The hit points are in the picture block. Open fsafe.mbl in the blocks editor and pick burr0: its Hit points is -5, and so is burr1's, so it hurts on either picture. A touch applies it once, and then the burr is gone.
  • The beep and the ouch face are Lami's own. Losing hit points starts their Hurt sequence (hero.chr, Sequences tab): the ouch picture and a short beep. You did not draw a flash; the sequence is a small picture change on Lami only.
  • The number is a second monster. The burr's When destroyed it becomes is monster 4, the number. It is born where the burr was, rises two blocks along a path and ends there (End -1). It is one picture, so it holds still as it rises. A number that blinked would be a flash, a small one.
  • The picture of the wrong way is a still sign made of ordinary blocks (panel.white in one.bbl). Nothing about it moves.
  • The walls. A hedge closes the room in at both ends.

The same trick, a monster that turns into a number, is in Score Popups.

pages.head: Level 2: Slow and Small
pages.html:
Level 2: Slow and Small

Two lamps stand on posts. The first one is dark for half a second and lit for half a second, once a second. The second pulses: it brightens in three small steps and dims in three, about once every 2.6 seconds. Both are amber, one block big, and neither is red or white.

A still picture by the third sign shows the wrong way: a big red screen blinking. It is a dull red with a slash through it. The last sign says that the door fades, and it does: Game-Maker fades the picture to black when you leave a scene and fades the next one in, so there is no white card between scenes.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 2 is made

  • A lamp is a ring of blocks. Open two.bbl and pick lampA.on. Its Next block is lampA.off and its Time is 9 ticks; lampA.off lasts 9 and turns back into lampA.on. 18 ticks is a second (there are 18.2), so that is one blink a second. Three a second would be a ring of 3 ticks.
  • The soft pulse is a ring of six blocks, lampB.s0 to lampB.s5, 8 ticks each. The glass goes dark, a little amber, more, full, and back through the same two steps. The two steps back need blocks of their own (s4 and s5 look like s2 and s1), because a block can only turn into one next block.
  • Small. A lamp is one 20 by 20 block on a screen of 312 by 196. The map holds the first block of each ring, lampA.start and lampB.start, which looks like the first step but lasts as long as its own Time the first time round.
  • Not red. The glass uses the gold ramp, from a dark amber to a pale one. The red picture on the sign is a dull brick color, still, and has a slash through it.
  • The fade is Game-Maker's own. PLAYGAME fades to black when a scene ends and fades the new palette in (FadeTo in code/GM/PLAYGAME.C). Do not put a white level card in front of it.

For other things that change by themselves, see Flicker and Flow, and for a block that warns before it acts, Warning First.

pages.head: Level 3: Storm, Held
pages.html:
Level 3: Storm, Held

The sky is a deep blue-gray. Every few seconds it lifts a little in two small steps, stays lifted for about a second, and settles back the same way. While it is held, a small pale bolt shows against it, and it goes when the sky settles. Nothing here strobes: the light never changes by much, and never more than once every five seconds.

Stand under the bolt and watch it once, then take the coins and go to the door.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 3 is made

  • The sky is a ring. Open three.bbl and pick st.sky.calm: it lasts 60 ticks and turns into st.sky.lift (4 ticks), then st.sky.hold (22 ticks), then st.sky.settle (4 ticks), then back to calm. Every sky block in the level and past its edges is the same block, so the whole sky changes on the same tick.
  • Small steps. The three colors are close: the brightest is not much lighter than the darkest. That is the point of the level. A change that big, on that much of the screen, is not a flash. A change from black to white across the sky would be.
  • Held, not strobed. The hold lasts 22 ticks, more than a second, and the cycle is 90 ticks. The sky changes four times in five seconds, never four in one.
  • The bolt is three blocks in a column (st.bolt0 to st.bolt2). Each is a ring on the same clock, and each draws the bolt only in its hold picture. A block can only turn into one next block, so everything on the sky that must change with it (the bolt, the coins, the posts of the signs, the doors) has its own ring of four blocks with the sky behind it in each color. Otherwise a pale rectangle would show around it while the sky changes.
  • The coins turn into st.sky.start when you touch them, which joins them to the sky's own ring at whatever step it is on.

pages.head: How to check your game
pages.html:
How to check your game

  1. Count. Play each level in the editor's Play and watch anything that changes by itself: a lamp, a sky, a torch, a sign. Count how many times it changes there and back in a second. Three or fewer is the line; fewer is kinder.
  2. Read the times. Open the Blocks tab. A block that turns into another has a Time in ticks, and there are 18.2 ticks in a second. A flash needs two changes (there and back), so a ring of two blocks that each last 3 ticks flashes 3 times a second, and one that lasts 2 ticks flashes more than 4.
  3. Run the Level check. Its flashing finding names animated blocks that swap faster than three flashes a second over a quarter of the screen or more. It is a suggestion: it measures blocks, not the picture.
  4. Look at the size. A small flash is gentler than a big one. Anything that flashes over a quarter of the screen, or is a large red, needs to be slow, or a different cue.
  5. Look at the colors. A change between two near-equal colors is not a flash. A change between black and white, or to and from a saturated red, is.
  6. Offer another cue. A hit should also have a sound, a number or a shape, so no one needs to see a flash to know.

For a whole game, npx vite-node ../games/kit/flashCheck.ts <id> replays its walkthrough and counts large light changes in every second, using the W3C's WCAG 2.3.1 test on each 320 by 200 frame. It is advice, not a verdict: it cannot know how big your player's screen is.

pages.head: What Game-Maker cannot do
pages.html:
What Game-Maker cannot do

  • It cannot play a sound when a block changes. A hit has a sound because it is Lami's Hurt sequence, and thunder has none here.
  • It cannot fade one sky color into another smoothly. A block changes picture all at once; a soft change is a ring of small steps, one block each.
  • It cannot flash only part of a picture by itself. Everything of one block kind changes on one tick, so a ring is on one clock for the whole level.
  • It cannot count a block's flashes for you, and it does not stop you from making a fast ring. The Level check only warns.
  • A block turns into one next block, so a ring that goes up and back down needs a block for each step in each direction.
  • A monster's picture can blink faster than a block can, because its pictures have their own times: be as careful with a monster's two frames as with a ring.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

Try one change at a time, and play after each:

  • In two.bbl, change lampA.on's Time from 9 to 3 and lampA.off's from 9 to 3. That is three flashes a second: the line. Then check with the Level check, and put it back.
  • Lengthen lampB.s0 to s5 for a slower pulse.
  • In three.bbl, change st.sky.hold's Time to hold the lift longer, or st.sky.calm's for a longer rest.
  • In the monsters editor, change the burr's Hit points block to take 10, or give the number another picture of your own.
  • Draw a different hurt picture for Lami in the character blocks.

The home page's Starters tab has more small games like this one.

box.back: A small explorer in a red beanie has three short rooms that show how to make a game that never relies on a flash. A hit gets a beep, a face, a number and fewer hit points. A warning lamp blinks slowly and small. A storm sky lifts a little and holds. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and change a time.
features: A hit shown four ways, and none of them a flash
A lamp that blinks once a second and one that pulses softly
A storm sky that lifts, holds and settles
Made to be copied and taken apart

blurb: Three short levels about making a game that is easy on the eyes. Some players can get sick from fast flashing, and some people have seizures from flashing light, so a game should never rely on it. Level 1 shows a hit without a flash: a beep, an ouch face, a number that rises and fewer hit points. Level 2 blinks a small amber lamp once a second and pulses another in soft steps. Level 3 lifts a dark sky a little, holds it, and lets it settle. Signs and still pictures show the wrong way, and the simple rules: no more than 3 flashes in a second, no big red flashes, keep flashing small, and offer other cues. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change a time.
